blocks.text: Programme planning for an ECCE centre means organising suitable activities, routines and experiences according to the developmental needs of young children.

Programme planning involves deciding objectives, selecting activities, arranging a daily routine (arrival, free play, circle time, outdoor play, meals, rest, story time, departure), preparing materials, organising space (activity corners like reading, art, blocks and dolls), and evaluating children's progress.
Good planning balances active and quiet activities, indoor and outdoor play, individual and group activities, and teacher-guided and child-initiated activities.

sections.title: Principles of Programme Planning
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Planning should be child-centred, flexible, balanced, age-appropriate, activity-based and suited to local needs and available resources.

Principles: (1) child-centred and developmentally appropriate; (2) holistic - covering all domains of development; (3) play-based and activity-based; (4) flexible and responsive to children's interests; (5) balanced; (6) based on local culture, language and resources; (7) inclusive; (8) involving parents and community; (9) continuous observation and assessment without formal tests.
Planning should move from simple to complex and from known to unknown and allow children to learn through exploration and experience.

sections.title: Long-term Planning
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Long-term planning organises broad goals, themes and activities over an extended period.

Long-term planning covers a year or a term. It sets overall goals for development, selects themes for each month (such as myself, my family, animals, plants, seasons, festivals, transport), plans special events and outings, and allocates resources.
It provides direction and continuity and ensures that all areas of development are covered over the year.

sections.title: Theme-based Short-term Planning
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Short-term planning organises activities around a particular theme for a shorter period and connects different learning experiences.

Short-term or theme-based planning covers a week or a few days around a theme like 'fruits' or 'rain'. Activities across areas are linked to the theme: stories and rhymes about fruits (language), counting fruits (numeracy), drawing and colouring fruits (art), tasting and sorting (sensory and science), and role play of a fruit shop (social skills).
Theme-based planning integrates learning, maintains children's interest and connects learning to daily life.

sections.title: Low-cost and No-cost Play Materials
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Useful play and learning materials can be prepared from inexpensive, locally available and waste materials, reducing cost and encouraging creativity.

Examples: bottle caps and seeds for counting; old boxes for building blocks; cloth and paper for puppets; old newspapers and magazines for collage; plastic bottles for musical shakers; leaves, stones and sticks for sorting and nature activities; clay from the local area for modelling.
Benefits: low cost, easy availability, environmental awareness (reuse), creativity of teachers and children, and connection with local culture. Materials must be safe, clean and non-toxic.

sections.title: Meeting Basic Personal Needs
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: ECCE activities should support children's basic needs such as safety, cleanliness, food habits, independence and healthy daily routines.

Children should be helped to develop self-help skills such as washing hands, using the toilet, eating independently, dressing, keeping belongings in place and cleanliness habits. Regular meals, rest and a safe environment are necessary.
These routines build independence, confidence and good habits. Teachers should be patient and encouraging, and coordinate with parents to maintain consistency between home and school.

sections.title: Storytelling
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Storytelling develops listening, imagination, vocabulary and interest in language.
Stories may be told using puppets, pictures, flannel boards, gestures and voice modulation. Folk tales, animal stories and local stories are popular with young children.

Benefits: develops listening skills and attention span, vocabulary and language, imagination and creativity, moral values, understanding of sequence and cause-effect, and emotional expression. Children can be encouraged to retell stories and act them out.

sections.title: Nursery Rhymes
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Nursery rhymes support language, rhythm, memory, enjoyment and participation.
Nursery rhymes are short, rhythmic poems with repetition and actions, such as 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star', and local rhymes in the mother tongue.

Benefits: they develop phonological awareness (sounds and rhythm), vocabulary, memory, pronunciation, motor coordination (through actions), group participation and joy in learning. Rhymes in the mother tongue connect children to their culture.

sections.title: Play with Materials
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Activities with blocks, toys, pictures, clay and other materials help children explore, create and develop physical and cognitive skills.

Examples: block building, sand and water play, clay modelling, puzzles, beads threading, colouring and painting, cutting and pasting, playing with dolls and kitchen sets, and simple science materials like magnets.
Benefits: development of fine and gross motor skills, eye-hand coordination, concepts of size, shape, colour and number, creativity, problem-solving and social skills through sharing.

sections.title: Play without Materials
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text: Games, movement, singing, imitation and group activities can promote physical, social and language development without special materials.
Examples: running, jumping, hopping, dancing, action songs, imitation games (walking like animals), circle games, hide and seek, 'Simon says', finger play, dramatisation and traditional games.

Benefits: physical fitness and gross motor development, listening and following instructions, social skills, cooperation, rule-following, self-expression and imagination. Such activities are especially useful where materials are scarce.

sections.title: Perspectives on ECCE in India
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Early Childhood Care and Education provides care and learning experiences during the early years, a period of rapid development. Its objectives include physical, emotional, social, language and intellectual development and preparation for later schooling.

The syllabus includes the National Policy on Education 1986 and the Yash Pal Committee in relation to ECCE. It also covers programmes and services for young children and the roles of ICCW and CSWB.

ECCE is therefore understood as a combination of care, development and education rather than simply early academic teaching.

Meaning and importance: ECCE refers to care, health, nutrition and education of children from birth to about eight years. Since most brain development happens in these years, quality ECCE improves school readiness, learning, health and later life outcomes, and reduces inequality.
Objectives: Holistic physical, emotional, social, language, cognitive and creative development, development of good habits and self-help skills, and smooth transition to primary school.

Policy perspectives: The National Policy on Education 1986 described ECCE as a crucial input for primary education and recommended a play-based, holistic approach integrated with ICDS and day-care centres. The Yash Pal Committee (1993) recommended abolition of tests and interviews for admission, no formal teaching or homework at the pre-primary stage and use of the mother tongue. NEP 2020 includes three years of pre-school in the Foundational Stage.
Agencies and services: ICDS/Anganwadis, ICCW, CSWB, government pre-primary sections, NGOs and private nursery schools provide services such as nutrition, health, crèches and pre-school education.

sections.title: Types of ECCE Centres
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Nursery programmes provide organised care and early learning before primary school. Kindergarten emphasizes play, songs, activities and experiences suitable for young children. Montessori education uses a prepared environment and special materials to encourage self-directed learning.

Anganwadi centres provide early childhood services under the ICDS framework. These types differ in organisation and method, but all aim to support development during early childhood.
Nursery schools: Developed by the McMillan sisters, nursery schools provide care, health, play and social experiences for children aged about 2 to 5 in a homely environment.
Kindergarten: Froebel's kindergarten (1837) treats the school as a garden and the teacher as a gardener. It uses gifts, occupations, songs, games and stories, emphasising self-activity and play.

Montessori: Maria Montessori's Children's House (1907) uses a prepared environment, self-correcting didactic apparatus, exercises of practical life and sense training. The child learns through auto-education while the teacher observes and guides.

Anganwadi: The Anganwadi centre under ICDS provides supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-ups, referral services, pre-school education and health and nutrition education. It is the largest ECCE system in India and is being strengthened under NEP 2020 and Mission Poshan 2.0.

sections.title: Programme Planning for ECCE
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Programme planning organises activities and routines so that ECCE objectives can be achieved. Planning should be child-centred, flexible, balanced and suitable to age, local conditions and available resources.

Long-term planning sets broader goals over an extended period, while theme-based short-term planning connects activities around a selected theme. Teachers can also prepare play materials from low-cost, no-cost and waste materials.

Good planning creates variety while maintaining a predictable and safe routine for young children.
Meaning: Programme planning in ECCE is the organisation of goals, activities, materials, space and time so that young children develop holistically.
Principles: Plans should be child-centred, developmentally appropriate, play-based, holistic, flexible, balanced, inclusive, based on local culture and resources, and should involve parents.

Types of planning: Long-term planning sets yearly or term goals and themes; theme-based short-term planning links activities in language, numeracy, art, science and social skills around a theme for a week or a few days. A daily routine balances free play, group time, outdoor play, meals, rest and stories.

Materials: Low-cost and no-cost materials made from waste and local resources - boxes, bottle caps, seeds, cloth, leaves and clay - make ECCE affordable and encourage creativity and environmental awareness.

sections.title: Play Activities in ECCE
context: EDU 204 – EARLY CHILDHOOD CARE AND EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Play is a central means of learning in early childhood. Activities should support basic personal needs and encourage independence and healthy habits. Storytelling and nursery rhymes develop language, imagination and memory.

Play with materials such as blocks, toys, clay and pictures supports exploration, creativity and motor development. Activities without materials, including movement, singing, imitation and group games, also develop physical and social abilities.

ECCE activities should therefore be enjoyable, developmentally appropriate and connected with the needs of the whole child.
Importance of play: Play is the natural way young children learn. It develops the body, mind, language, emotions and social skills, and gives joy and confidence.
Meeting personal needs: Activities and routines that develop self-help skills like handwashing, eating, dressing and toilet habits build independence and good health habits.
Language activities: Storytelling and nursery rhymes develop listening, vocabulary, imagination, memory, rhythm and moral values. Children can retell, dramatise and sing along.

Play with and without materials: Play with blocks, clay, puzzles, sand, water and art materials develops fine motor skills, concepts and creativity; play without materials - running, dancing, action songs, imitation and traditional games - develops gross motor skills, cooperation and rule-following. A good ECCE programme uses both types in a balanced way.
